title: Fables 1–53
author: Aesop
description: Chambry's text of the first fifty-three fables. Short, repetitive, and each one finishes in a sitting. Hand-annotated, with contextual word glosses from the Perseus annotators.

tr.aesop:2: By the bad things the good things were driven out, as being weak;
tr.aesop:3: and into heaven they went up.
tr.aesop:4: And the good things asked Zeus how they might be with men.
tr.aesop:5: And he said that not all together with one another, but one by one, they should come upon men.
tr.aesop:6: For this reason the bad things come upon men continually, as being near, but the good things more slowly, coming down from heaven.
tr.aesop:7: That of good things no one quickly obtains a share, but by the bad things each man is struck every day.

tr.aesop:9: Someone, having made a wooden Hermes and having brought it into the market, was trying to sell it;
tr.aesop:10: and since no buyer was approaching, wishing to call out some, he shouted that he was selling a god who does good and is a giver of profit.
tr.aesop:11: And when one of those who happened to be present said to him:
tr.aesop:12: "You there, why do you sell this one, he being such, when you ought to enjoy the benefits from him?"
tr.aesop:13: He answered that "I need some quick benefit, but he himself is accustomed to procure his gains slowly."
tr.aesop:14: For a man greedy for shameful gain and not even having given thought to the gods, the story is fitting.

tr.aesop:16: An eagle and a fox, having made friendship with one another, decided to live near each other, making their close association a confirmation of friendship.
tr.aesop:17: And so the one, having gone up onto a very tall tree, made a nest;
tr.aesop:18: and the other, having gone into the bush lying beneath, gave birth.
tr.aesop:19: When she had once gone out to feed, the eagle, being at a loss for food, having flown down into the bush and having snatched up the offspring, feasted on them with his own chicks.
tr.aesop:20: The fox, having returned, when she learned what had been done, was not so much grieved over the death of her young as over the revenge;
tr.aesop:21: for being a land animal, she was unable to pursue a winged creature.
tr.aesop:22: Therefore, standing far off, which alone is left to the powerless and weak, she cursed her enemy.
tr.aesop:23: And it happened that he, for his impiety toward the friendship, before long paid the penalty;
tr.aesop:24: for when some people were sacrificing a goat in the country, having flown down, from the altar he carried up a burning entrail;
tr.aesop:25: When this had been carried to the nest, a violent wind, falling upon it, kindled a bright flame from a thin and old twig.
tr.aesop:26: And because of this the chicks, burnt up (for the fledglings were still not fully grown), fell down onto the ground.
tr.aesop:27: And the fox, running up, in the sight of the eagle devoured them all.
tr.aesop:28: The story shows that those who break faith in friendship, even if they escape the punishment of those they have wronged because of the latters' weakness, yet at any rate do not ward off the vengeance from god.

tr.aesop:29: The eagle and the dung beetle.
tr.aesop:30: An eagle was chasing a hare.
tr.aesop:31: And the hare, being destitute of anyone who would help, seeing a dung beetle, the only one whom the occasion provided, begged this one.
tr.aesop:32: And the beetle, having encouraged him, when he saw the eagle coming near, urged it not to carry off his suppliant.
tr.aesop:33: And that one, disregarding his smallness, in the sight of the beetle feasted on the hare.
tr.aesop:34: And the beetle, from that time bearing a grudge, kept on watching the eagle's nests and, whenever that one laid eggs, rising up aloft, he rolled the eggs out and smashed them, until, driven out from everywhere, the eagle fled for refuge to Zeus (for the bird is sacred to the god) and begged him to provide it a safe place for raising chicks.
tr.aesop:35: And when Zeus had permitted it to lay its eggs in his own lap, the beetle, having seen this, having made a ball of dung, flew up and, getting over Zeus's lap, let it drop there.
tr.aesop:36: And Zeus, wishing to shake off the dung, when he stood up, threw out the eggs without noticing.
tr.aesop:37: And from that time they say that, at the season when the dung-beetles appear, the eagles do not nest.
tr.aesop:38: The story teaches us to despise no one, considering that no one is so powerless that, having been insulted, he cannot ever avenge himself.

tr.aesop:39: The Eagle and the Jackdaw and the Shepherd.
tr.aesop:40: An eagle, swooping down from some high rock, snatched a lamb;
tr.aesop:41: and a jackdaw, having seen this, out of envy wanted to imitate it;
tr.aesop:42: and so, letting itself down with much whirring, it was carried onto a ram.
tr.aesop:43: But its claws having become entangled in the fleece, being unable to lift itself up, it kept flapping until the shepherd, having perceived what had happened, running up seized it and, having clipped its wing-feathers, when evening came on, brought it to his own children.
tr.aesop:44: And when they asked what the bird was, he said:
tr.aesop:45: "As I clearly know, a jackdaw, but as it itself wishes, an eagle."
tr.aesop:46: Thus rivalry with those who are superior, besides achieving nothing, also gains laughter on top of misfortunes.

tr.aesop:47: The Eagle with Its Feathers Plucked and the Fox.
tr.aesop:48: An eagle was once caught by a man, who, having at once plucked its feathers, let it stay in the house with the poultry.
tr.aesop:49: And he was downcast from grief.
tr.aesop:50: But someone else, having bought him, immediately gave the eagle back his feathers.
tr.aesop:51: And he, having flown up and snatched a hare, brought it at once as a gift to his benefactor.
tr.aesop:52: A fox, having seen this, cried out:
tr.aesop:53: "Do not you entertain this one, but the first, lest the same man, having hunted you again, once more strip your feathers bare."
tr.aesop:54: The fable shows that one must give good returns to benefactors, but flee from the wicked.

tr.aesop:55: The eagle shot with an arrow.
tr.aesop:56: Above a rock an eagle was sitting, seeking to hunt hares.
tr.aesop:57: And someone, shooting with a bow, struck him, and the arrow went in;
tr.aesop:58: but the notch with the feathers stood before his eyes.
tr.aesop:59: And he, having seen it, said:
tr.aesop:60: "This too is another grief to me, to die by my own feathers."
tr.aesop:61: That the sting of grief is more terrible whenever someone is endangered by his own people.

tr.aesop:63: A nightingale, sitting on a certain high oak, was singing according to her custom.
tr.aesop:64: And a hawk, having seen her, since he was at a loss for food, flying down upon her, seized her.
tr.aesop:65: And she, being about to be killed, begged him to let her go, saying that she by herself was not enough to fill a hawk's stomach;
tr.aesop:66: but he must, if he was at a loss for food, turn to the larger of the birds.
tr.aesop:68: "But I would be senseless, if, letting go the food ready in my hands, I should chase things not yet appearing."
tr.aesop:69: So also among men those are unreasoning who, through hope of greater things, let go the things that are in their hands.

tr.aesop:71: A swallow advised a nightingale to be under the same roof and dwelling together with men, as she herself was.
tr.aesop:73: "I do not wish to remember the grief of my old misfortunes, and for this reason I dwell in the deserts."
tr.aesop:74: [That] the one grieved by some misfortune wishes also to flee the place where the grief happened.

tr.aesop:76: At Athens a debtor man, being asked by the lender for the debt, at first kept begging him to give him a delay, claiming to be without means.
tr.aesop:77: But when he did not persuade him, bringing forward a sow which alone he had, in his presence he was selling it.
tr.aesop:78: And a buyer having come up and asking whether the sow was a breeder, that man said that not only did she give birth, but also marvellously:
tr.aesop:79: for at the Mysteries she brought forth females, and at the Panathenaea males.
tr.aesop:80: And the buyer being astounded at the statement, the lender said:
tr.aesop:82: for this one will also bear you kids at the Dionysia."
tr.aesop:83: The story shows that many, for the sake of their own gain, do not hesitate to bear false witness even to impossible things.

tr.aesop:85: An Ethiopian someone bought, thinking that his colour was such through the neglect of the one who had him before.
tr.aesop:86: And having taken him home, he applied all the soaps to him, and with all baths he tried to clean him.
tr.aesop:87: And the colour he was not able to change, but he caused him to fall sick through the toil.
tr.aesop:88: The fable shows that natures remain as they came forth at the beginning.

tr.aesop:90: A cat, having seized a cock, wanted to devour him with a reasonable excuse.
tr.aesop:91: And so, beginning, he accused him, saying that he was troublesome to men, crowing by night and not even allowing them to get sleep.
tr.aesop:92: When he said that he does this for their benefit, for he wakes them up to their accustomed works, he said a second time:
tr.aesop:93: "But you are also impious toward nature, mounting both sisters and mother."
tr.aesop:94: When he said that this too he does for the benefit of his masters, for he causes many eggs to be laid for them, that one, at a loss, said:
tr.aesop:95: "If then you always have plenty of pretexts, I will none the less eat you."
tr.aesop:96: The story shows that a wicked nature, choosing to do wrong, even if it cannot with a reasonable pretext, does evil without disguise.

tr.aesop:98: In a certain house there were many mice.
tr.aesop:99: And a cat, having learned this, came there and, catching them one by one, kept devouring them.
tr.aesop:100: And the mice, being continually consumed, slipped down into their holes, and the cat, no longer being able to reach them, decided that it was necessary to lure them out by a trick.
tr.aesop:101: Therefore, having climbed up onto a certain peg and having hung himself down from there, he pretended to be dead.
tr.aesop:102: But one of the mice, peeping out, when he saw him, said:
tr.aesop:103: "But, you there, to you at least, even if you become a sack, I will not come near."
tr.aesop:104: The story shows that the prudent among men, whenever they have experienced the wickedness of some, are no longer by their pretenses [these] deceived.

tr.aesop:106: A cat, having heard that in a certain farmstead birds were sick, having disguised himself as a doctor and having taken up the instruments suited to the profession, arrived, and standing before the farmstead asked them how they were.
tr.aesop:108: "Well," they said, "if you get away from here."
tr.aesop:109: So also among men the wicked do not escape the notice of the sensible, even if they pretend to goodness as much as possible.

tr.aesop:111: A goatherd was calling the goats back to the fold.
tr.aesop:112: But one of them was left behind, grazing on something sweet.
tr.aesop:113: And the shepherd, having thrown a stone, broke her horn, having aimed well.
tr.aesop:114: And he begged the goat not to tell this to the master.
tr.aesop:116: "Even if I keep silent, how shall I hide it?
tr.aesop:117: For plain to all is my horn broken."
tr.aesop:118: That, when the cause is plain, it is not possible to hide it.

tr.aesop:120: A goat and a donkey someone was keeping.
tr.aesop:121: And the goat, having envied the donkey because of the abundance of its food, said that it was punished without end, at one time grinding, at another carrying burdens, and advised it, having made itself seem seized by a fit, to fall down into some pit and obtain rest.
tr.aesop:122: And he, having believed and having fallen, was badly crushed.
tr.aesop:123: And the master, having called the doctor, asked him to help.
tr.aesop:124: And he said to pour in for him a goat's lung, and so to obtain health.
tr.aesop:125: And having sacrificed the goat, they treated the donkey.
tr.aesop:126: That whoever contrives tricks against another becomes of his own evils the originator.

tr.aesop:128: A goatherd, having driven his goats out to pasture, when he saw them mixed with wild ones, evening coming on, drove them all into his own cave.
tr.aesop:129: And on the next day, a great storm having come, not being able to lead them to the usual pasture, he tended them inside, to his own throwing moderate food only so as not to starve, but for the strangers heaping up more so as to make them also his own.
tr.aesop:130: And the storm having ceased, when he led them all out to pasture, the wild ones, having taken to the mountains, fled.
tr.aesop:131: And when the shepherd accused them of ingratitude, if indeed they, having obtained more abundant care, were leaving him, they said, having turned around:
tr.aesop:132: "But for this very reason we are all the more on our guard:
tr.aesop:133: For if you honoured us, who came to you yesterday, above those long with you, it is clear that, if others also approach you after this, you will prefer them to us."
tr.aesop:134: The story shows that one must not welcome the friendships of those who honour us, the newcomers, above their old friends, considering that, even if, while we are of long standing with them, they make friends with others, they will prefer those.

tr.aesop:136: A master loved an ugly and ill-mannered slave-girl.
tr.aesop:137: And she, receiving gold, adorned herself splendidly and kept engaging in fights with her own mistress;
tr.aesop:138: and she sacrificed continually to Aphrodite and prayed to her as to the one making her beautiful.
tr.aesop:139: And she, appearing in sleep to the slave-girl, said that she should not be grateful to her as the one making her beautiful, "but I am angry and enraged at that man to whom you appear beautiful."
tr.aesop:140: That those who are rich through shameful means should not be puffed up, and especially if they are low-born and ill-favoured [to greater shame].

tr.aesop:142: Aesop the fable-writer, being at leisure, went into a shipyard.
tr.aesop:143: And when the shipwrights were both mocking him and calling him out to an answer, Aesop said that in ancient times chaos and water came into being, and that Zeus, wishing to bring forth also the element of earth, urged her to gulp down the sea three times.
tr.aesop:144: And she, having begun, first revealed the mountains, and the second time, gulping it down, laid bare the plains too;
tr.aesop:145: "And if she decides to drink up the water a third time too, your craft will become useless."
tr.aesop:146: The story shows that those who mock their betters unwittingly draw on themselves greater troubles from them.

tr.aesop:148: While two cocks were fighting over hens, the one routed the other.
tr.aesop:149: And the defeated one, going away into a shady place, hid himself;
tr.aesop:150: but the victor, rising up high and standing on a high wall, crowed with a loud voice.
tr.aesop:151: And at once an eagle, swooping down, snatched him away.
tr.aesop:152: But the one hidden in darkness from then on mounted the hens without fear.
tr.aesop:153: The fable shows that the Lord opposes the proud, but to the humble gives grace.

tr.aesop:155: A man who had cocks at his house, when he came upon a tame partridge being sold, bought it and brought it home to be reared together with them.
tr.aesop:156: But when they struck it and chased it away, the partridge was disheartened, thinking that it was despised for this reason, that it was of another race.
tr.aesop:157: Having paused a little, when he saw the cocks fighting among themselves and not leaving off before they had bloodied one another, he said to himself:
tr.aesop:158: "But I, for my part, am no longer vexed at being beaten by them;
tr.aesop:159: for I see them not even keeping their hands off themselves."
tr.aesop:160: The story shows that sensible people bear easily the insults of their neighbours whenever they see them not even keeping their hands off their own kin.

tr.aesop:162: Fishermen, having gone out for a catch and having toiled a long time, caught nothing;
tr.aesop:163: and sitting in the boat they were disheartened.
tr.aesop:164: Meanwhile a tuna, being chased and rushing along with a great whirring, leapt unawares into the boat.
tr.aesop:165: And they, having seized it and having driven off to the city, sold it.
tr.aesop:166: Thus often what skill did not provide, this chance has bestowed.

tr.aesop:169: And as it was heavy, they rejoiced and danced, thinking the catch to be great.
tr.aesop:170: But when, having dragged it onto the shore, they found few of the fish, but the net full of stones and other stuff, they were not moderately dejected, not so much distressed at what had happened as because they had also anticipated the opposite.
tr.aesop:171: And a certain one among them, being old, said:
tr.aesop:173: for of joy, as it seems, sister is grief, and we, having rejoiced beforehand so much, had to suffer by all means something painful too."
tr.aesop:174: So then we too must, seeing the changeableness of life, not always exult in the same circumstances, reckoning that out of much fair weather it is necessary that a storm also arise.

tr.aesop:176: A fisherman experienced in pipe-playing, having taken up pipes and the nets, came to the sea, and standing on a certain projecting rock, at first he sang, thinking that of their own accord at the sweet sound the fish would leap out to him.
tr.aesop:177: But when, while he strained for a long time, no result was achieved, setting aside the pipes he took up the casting-net and, casting it into the water, caught many fish.
tr.aesop:178: And throwing them out from the net onto the shore, when he saw them writhing, he said:
tr.aesop:179: "O most wretched creatures, you, when I was piping, did not dance, but now, when I have stopped, this you do."
tr.aesop:180: For those who do something out of season the story is well-timed.

tr.aesop:181: A Fisherman (and the big and small fish).
tr.aesop:182: A fisherman, having drawn out of the sea the net for catching, became master of the big fish and spread these out on the land;
tr.aesop:183: but the smaller of the fish slipped away through the holes into the sea.
tr.aesop:184: That safety is easy for those not greatly fortunate, but the one who is great in reputation you would rarely see escaping the dangers.

tr.aesop:186: A fisherman, having let down the net, brought up a sprat.
tr.aesop:187: And when she begged him for the present to let her go, since she happens to be small, but later, when she had grown, to catch her for greater profit, the fisherman said:
tr.aesop:188: "But I would be most foolish, if, having let go the gain in hand, I were to chase an uncertain hope."
tr.aesop:189: The story shows that more to be chosen is the present gain, even if it is small, than the expected one, even if it is great.

tr.aesop:191: A fisherman was fishing in a certain river.
tr.aesop:192: And then, having stretched out the nets, when he had enclosed the stream on each side, having tied a stone to a fine cord, he was beating the water, so that the fish, fleeing, might fall unguardedly into the meshes.
tr.aesop:193: And one of those dwelling around the place, having seen him doing this, was blaming him for muddying the river and not allowing them to drink clear water.
tr.aesop:195: "But if the river is not stirred up thus, it will be necessary for me to die starving."
tr.aesop:196: So also the demagogues of cities then most of all do their work, whenever they bring their fatherlands round into factions.

tr.aesop:198: The halcyon is a bird fond of solitude, through everything living on the sea.
tr.aesop:199: This bird is said, guarding against the hunts of men, to make its nest on rocks beside the sea.
tr.aesop:200: And indeed once, being about to give birth, she came to a certain headland, and having seen a rock by the sea, there she was making her nest.
tr.aesop:201: And when she had gone out once for feeding, it happened that the sea, raised into waves by a violent wind, was lifted up as far as the nest and, flooding it, destroyed the chicks.
tr.aesop:202: And the halcyon, having come back, when she learned what had happened, said:
tr.aesop:203: "But I am wretched, who, guarding against the land as treacherous, fled for refuge to this, which has become much more untrustworthy to me."
tr.aesop:204: So also some of men, guarding against their enemies, unawares fall in with friends much harsher than their enemies.

tr.aesop:206: Once foxes gathered at the Maeander river, wanting to drink from it.
tr.aesop:207: But because the water was rushing along with a roar, though urging one another on, they did not dare to go in.
tr.aesop:208: But one of them, holding forth to belittle the rest and mocking their cowardice, judging herself nobler, boldly leapt into the water.
tr.aesop:209: And when the current had swept her down into the middle, and the rest, standing by the bank of the river, said to her: "Do not leave us, but turn and show us the way in by which we will be able to drink without danger," she, being carried away, said:
tr.aesop:210: "I have a reply for Miletus, and I wish to carry it there;
tr.aesop:211: but when I come back I will show you."
tr.aesop:212: Against those who through boastfulness bring danger on themselves.

tr.aesop:213: A fox swollen in the belly.
tr.aesop:214: A starving fox, when she saw in a certain hollow of an oak bread and meat left behind by some shepherds, went in and ate them up.
tr.aesop:215: But, swollen in the belly, since she could not get out, she groaned and lamented.
tr.aesop:216: And another fox passing by there, when she heard her groaning, came up and asked the cause.
tr.aesop:217: Having learned what had happened, she said to her:
tr.aesop:218: "But stay meanwhile you here, until you become such as you were when you went in, and so you will easily come out."
tr.aesop:219: The story shows that the difficult among affairs time resolves.

tr.aesop:221: A fox, climbing a fence, when she was about to slip, took hold of a bramble.
tr.aesop:222: Having had the sole of her foot torn and being terribly affected, she blamed it because, having fled to it as to a helper, she had found it worse.
tr.aesop:224: "But you were mistaken in your wits, you there, in wanting to take hold of me, who myself am accustomed to take hold of everything."
tr.aesop:225: So also among men foolish are all who flee for refuge to those as helpers to whom doing wrong is more inborn.

tr.aesop:227: A fox, being hungry, when she saw from a certain tree-trained vine grapes hanging, wanted to get hold of them and could not.
tr.aesop:228: Going away, she said to herself:
tr.aesop:230: So also some of men, not being able to attain things through weakness, blame the circumstances.

tr.aesop:232: [A fig tree was beside a road.]
tr.aesop:233: A fox [and], having seen a snake sleeping, envied its length;
tr.aesop:234: and wishing to be made equal to it, lying down beside it she tried to stretch herself out, until, straining too hard, she burst before she knew it.
tr.aesop:235: This is what they suffer who compete against those stronger than them;
tr.aesop:236: for they themselves burst sooner than they are able to reach those.

tr.aesop:238: A fox, fleeing hunters, when she saw a certain woodcutter, begged him to hide her.
tr.aesop:239: And he advised her, having gone into his own hut, to hide.
tr.aesop:240: And not long after, the hunters having arrived and inquiring of the woodcutter whether he had seen a fox passing by here, he with his voice denied having seen her, but with his hand, nodding, he indicated where she was hidden.
tr.aesop:241: They paying no heed to what he signalled by nodding, but trusting what he said, the fox, seeing them gone away, came out and went off without a word.
tr.aesop:242: When the woodcutter reproached her because, though saved by him, she had not even by a word acknowledged him, she said:
tr.aesop:243: "But I would have thanked you, if you had the works of your hand and your ways like your words."
tr.aesop:244: This story one might use toward those people who promise good things plainly, but through their deeds do base things.

tr.aesop:246: A fox and a crocodile were disputing about noble birth.
tr.aesop:247: When the crocodile had related much about the splendour of his ancestors and at last said that he was from fathers who had been gymnasiarchs, the fox said:
tr.aesop:248: "But even if you do not say so, from your skin you are plainly one who has been trained in the gymnasium for many years."
tr.aesop:249: So too of lying people the proof is the facts.

tr.aesop:251: A fox, having gone into a flock of sheep and picked up one of the suckling lambs, pretended to kiss it.
tr.aesop:252: Being asked by a dog why she was doing this, "I am nursing it," she said, "and playing with it."
tr.aesop:254: "And now, if you do not let the lamb go from yourself, I will bring upon you the things of dogs."
tr.aesop:255: Against a man who is a rogue and a foolish thief the story is timely.

tr.aesop:257: A fox and a leopard were quarrelling about beauty.
tr.aesop:258: And as the leopard at every point was putting forward the variegation of her body, the fox, interrupting, said:
tr.aesop:259: "And how much more beautiful than you am I, who not in my body, but in my soul have been made variegated."
tr.aesop:260: The story shows that better than bodily beauty is the adornment of the mind.

tr.aesop:261: A fox and a monkey chosen king.
tr.aesop:262: In an assembly of the irrational animals a monkey, having danced and won approval, was elected king by them.
tr.aesop:263: And a fox, having envied him, when she saw in a certain trap some meat lying, having led him there, was saying that having found a treasure she herself had not used it, but as a prize of the kingship for him she had kept it, and she was urging him to take it.
tr.aesop:264: And when he had approached carelessly and had been caught by the trap, and was blaming the fox as having set an ambush for him, she said:
tr.aesop:265: "O monkey, and do you, having such foolishness, reign over the irrational animals?"
tr.aesop:266: Thus those who set their hands to affairs without circumspection, on top of faring badly, also incur laughter.

tr.aesop:267: A fox and a monkey quarrelling about noble birth.
tr.aesop:268: A fox and a monkey, travelling in the same place, were quarrelling about noble birth.
tr.aesop:269: And while each was recounting many things, when they came to a certain place, there, having gazed, the monkey groaned aloud.
tr.aesop:270: And when the fox asked the reason, the monkey, having shown her the tombs, said:
tr.aesop:271: "But am I not to weep, seeing the gravestones of my father's freedmen and slaves?"
tr.aesop:273: "Well, lie as much as you wish;
tr.aesop:274: for none of these, having risen up, will refute you."
tr.aesop:275: Thus also among men the liars boast most at that time, whenever they do not have those who would refute them.

tr.aesop:277: A fox, having fallen into a well, remained there of necessity.
tr.aesop:278: And a goat, gripped by thirst, came to the same well;
tr.aesop:279: and having seen her, he asked whether the water was good;
tr.aesop:280: and she, welcoming the chance, launched into praise of the water, saying that the water was excellent, and urged him to come down.
tr.aesop:281: And when he had gone down without forethought because of his desire, at the same time as quenching his thirst he considered with the fox the way up.
tr.aesop:282: And the fox, taking him up, said:
tr.aesop:283: "I know something useful, if only you are willing for the safety of us both.
tr.aesop:284: Be willing, then, to plant your front feet against the wall and to set your horns upright, and I, having run up, will also pull you up."
tr.aesop:285: And when he had readily listened to her advice, the fox, leaping up by way of his legs and his shoulders and his horns, found herself at the mouth of the well, and having got out, she went off.
tr.aesop:286: And when the goat blamed her for having broken their agreement, she turned around and said to the goat:
tr.aesop:287: "You there, if you had as many wits as hairs in your beard, you would not have gone down before you had considered the way up."
tr.aesop:288: So also among men, the sensible ought first to consider the outcomes of matters, and then accordingly undertake them.

tr.aesop:289: The Fox with a Docked Tail.
tr.aesop:290: A fox, having had her tail cut off by some trap, since out of shame she thought she had a life not worth living, decided that she must bring the other foxes too into the same state, so that by the common misfortune she might hide her own defect.
tr.aesop:291: And so, having gathered them all, she urged them to cut off their tails, saying that not only is this unsightly, but also some superfluous weight has been fastened onto them.
tr.aesop:292: But one of them, answering, said:
tr.aesop:293: "You there, if this were not to your advantage, you would not have advised it to us."
tr.aesop:294: This story fits those who give advice to their neighbours not out of goodwill, but for what is advantageous to themselves.

tr.aesop:295: The Fox That Had Never Seen a Lion.
tr.aesop:296: A fox that had never seen a lion, when by some chance she met one, at first on seeing him was so thrown into confusion that she nearly died.
tr.aesop:297: And on meeting him a second time she was afraid, but not so much as before.
tr.aesop:298: And on seeing him a third time she grew so bold that she even went up to him and talked with him.
tr.aesop:299: The story shows that familiarity tames even fearsome things.

tr.aesop:301: A fox, having entered into a sculptor's workshop and searching through each of the things inside, when she came upon a tragic actor's mask, lifting this up said:
tr.aesop:302: "What a head, and it does not have a brain!"
tr.aesop:303: To a man magnificent in body but in soul unreasoning, the fable is fitting.

tr.aesop:305: Two men were fighting over which of the gods were greater, Theseus or Heracles.
tr.aesop:306: And the gods, angered at them, each took vengeance on the land of the other.
tr.aesop:307: That the strife of subordinates persuades the masters to be angry against their subjects.

tr.aesop:309: Someone, having killed a man, was being pursued by that man's kinsmen;
tr.aesop:310: and having come to the Nile river, a wolf having met him, being afraid he climbed up onto a tree lying beside the river and there was hiding.
tr.aesop:311: But having seen there a serpent rising up against him, he let himself down into the river;
tr.aesop:312: and in the river a crocodile feasted on him.
tr.aesop:313: The story shows that for the accursed among men neither the element of earth, nor of air, nor of water is safe.

tr.aesop:315: A poor man, being sick and in a bad way, when he had been given up by the doctors, prayed to the gods, promising to make a hecatomb and to dedicate offerings, if he should rise up again.
tr.aesop:316: And his wife (for she happened to be standing beside him) asking, "And from where will you pay these?", he said:
tr.aesop:317: "For do you think that I will rise up again, so that the gods may also demand these things of me?"
tr.aesop:318: The story shows that men easily promise those things which they do not expect to accomplish in deed.

tr.aesop:319: A cowardly man and the ravens.
tr.aesop:320: A cowardly man was going out to war.
tr.aesop:321: And when ravens cried out, putting down his weapons he kept still, then taking them up he went out again, and when they were crying again, he stopped and finally said:
tr.aesop:322: "You will croak, indeed, as loudly as you can;
tr.aesop:323: but me you will not taste."
tr.aesop:324: The fable is about the very cowardly.

tr.aesop:325: A man bitten by an ant, and Hermes.
tr.aesop:326: Once, seeing a ship sunk together with its men, someone was saying that the gods judge unjustly;
tr.aesop:327: for because of one impious man the innocent too had perished along with him.
tr.aesop:328: While he was saying these things, there being many ants in the place in which he happened to be standing, it came about that he was bitten by one.
tr.aesop:329: And he, bitten by one, trampled them all together.
tr.aesop:330: But Hermes, standing over him and striking him with his staff, said:
tr.aesop:331: "Then do you not put up with the gods being judges such as you are of the ants?"
tr.aesop:332: That no one should revile a god when misfortune has come upon him, but rather let him examine his own sins.

tr.aesop:333: A man and a difficult wife.
tr.aesop:334: Someone, having a wife very difficult in character toward all the household, wished to know whether toward her father's servants too she was disposed in the same way;
tr.aesop:335: whereupon, with a plausible pretext, he sent her to her father.
tr.aesop:336: And after a few days, when she had come back, he asked how the household had received her.
tr.aesop:337: When she said, "The cowherds and the shepherds looked askance at me," he said to her:
tr.aesop:338: "But, wife, if you were hated by these, who drive out the flocks at dawn and come in late, what must one expect about those with whom you spent the whole day?"
tr.aesop:339: Thus often from small things great things, and from evident things hidden things, are recognized.

tr.aesop:341: A mischievous man, having agreed with someone that he would show the oracle at Delphi to be false, when the appointed day arrived, taking a sparrow in his hand and covering it with his cloak, came to the temple and, standing opposite, asked whether he had something breathing in his hands or lifeless, wishing, if it said lifeless, to show the sparrow alive, but if breathing, to strangle it and bring it out.
tr.aesop:342: And the god, perceiving his crafty intention, said:
tr.aesop:344: for it rests with you whether this which you have is dead or alive."
tr.aesop:345: The story shows that the divine cannot be tampered with.

tr.aesop:347: A pentathlete, being reproached each time by the citizens for unmanliness, having once gone abroad and after a time returned, boasting said that, having done many brave deeds in other cities too, in Rhodes he had jumped such a jump that none of the Olympic victors could reach it;
tr.aesop:348: and he claimed that he would provide as witnesses of this those who had been present, if ever they should come to town.
tr.aesop:349: And one of those present, taking him up, said to him:
tr.aesop:350: "But, you there, if this is true, you have no need of witnesses;
tr.aesop:351: for here is both Rhodes and the leap."
tr.aesop:352: The story shows that where proof through deeds is at hand, about these things all talk is superfluous.

tr.aesop:353: A Middle-Aged Man and His Mistresses.
tr.aesop:354: A middle-aged man had two mistresses, of whom one was young, and the other old.
tr.aesop:355: And the one who was advanced in years, being ashamed to be intimate with one younger than herself, kept on, whenever he came to her, removing his black hairs.
tr.aesop:356: And the younger one, shrinking from having an old lover, kept pulling out his grey hairs.
tr.aesop:357: And so it happened to him, being plucked by both in turn, to become bald.
tr.aesop:358: So everywhere what is incongruous is harmful.

tr.aesop:360: A rich Athenian man was sailing with some others.
tr.aesop:361: And indeed, a violent storm having arisen and the ship having capsized, all the others were swimming to safety, but the Athenian, calling upon Athena at every turn, kept promising countless things, if he should be saved.
tr.aesop:362: But one of those shipwrecked with him, swimming alongside, said to him:
tr.aesop:363: "Along with Athena, you too move your hand."
tr.aesop:364: So then we too, along with calling upon the gods, must ourselves also act, thinking something out on our own behalf.
tr.aesop:365: For it is to be welcomed that those who are active obtain the goodwill of the gods, rather than that those neglecting themselves be saved by the divine powers.
tr.aesop:366: Those who fall into misfortunes must themselves also toil on their own behalf, and only then ask the god for help.
